[THOUGHT] The presentation is compatible with a fixed drug eruption (FDE)—recurrent well-demarcated red/violaceous macules on lips and dorsal hands that the patient links to taking oral medications, and described evolution from pink to darker brown. However, several core diagnostic elements are missing or contradictive: the patient cannot identify a reproducible temporal relationship (latency after ingestion) or confirm that lesions reappear at identical sites each time (the cardinal feature of FDE). The punch biopsy from an active lesion was reported as "Normal," which weakens the diagnosis (FDE usually shows interface dermatitis, necrotic keratinocytes, and pigment incontinence on H&E). There is also no clear documentation that naproxen was taken immediately before episodes—so assigning naproxen as the culprit is unsupported. Red-flag features that would mandate urgent change in management (widespread blistering, mucosal erosions, systemic symptoms suggesting SJS/TEN) were reportedly absent but need verification on exam.

Critical missing items:
- Clear medication timeline (including OTC/herbal, recent antibiotics) with exact timing relative to each episode.
- Latency from drug ingestion to lesion onset.
- Whether lesions reproducibly recur at the exact same anatomic sites.
- Whether lesions leave persistent hyperpigmentation between episodes.
- Full, detailed histopathology report or dermatopathologist review of slides (H&E description rather than single word "Normal").
- Photographs of typical lesions and exam documentation of mucosa/systemic signs.

[DECISION] INCOMPLETE

[FEEDBACK] To make a defensible diagnosis (or exclude FDE) collect the following specific information and tests:
1. Detailed medication chronology:
   - List all prescription, OTC, supplements, and recent antibiotics/vaccines with start/stop dates, dosages, and what was taken within 72 hours before each episode.
   - Ask patient to identify any single medication that has consistently preceded prior flares.

2. Precise timing and reproducibility:
   - For recent and prior episodes, document exact latency from ingestion to lesion appearance.
   - Ask whether lesions recur in identical locations each time and whether residual brown hyperpigmentation persists between flares.

3. Objective documentation and exam:
   - Full skin and mucosal exam during acute episode and when cleared; obtain standardized photographs of lesions (acute and residual hyperpigmentation).
   - Verify absence of systemic symptoms (fever, arthralgia, eye symptoms, or widespread blistering).

4. Pathology confirmation:
   - Request full H&E description from dermatopathology or have slide re-reviewed for interface dermatitis, necrotic keratinocytes, pigment incontinence, inflammatory infiltrate.
   - If uncertainty persists, consider repeat biopsy of an active lesion.

5. Diagnostic testing and specialist input:
   - Dermatology referral for evaluation.
   - If clinically indicated, consider patch testing on residual hyperpigmented site and/or supervised oral provocation challenge to identify the culprit (only in controlled setting).
   - If severe or atypical features appear, rule out SJS/TEN and other diagnoses (lichenoid drug eruption, pigmented purpura, contact/mucosal disease).

Collecting these items will allow confirmation of FDE and identification of the offending agent, or will redirect to an alternative diagnosis.
